title: Seeking perspectives on game dev workflow pre-and post-LLM
author: jimbo-slim
selftext:
Hello all,

I am looking to get some perspectives from the more seasoned game developers/artists/engineers on how LLM's and associated tools like Claude Code or Codex etc have changed the game development landscape.

I am a professional computer scientist myself and I have seen firsthand how work can be accelerated by these tools. I am also a casual gamer and in the last year have been vibe coding games in Unreal with the help of these tools.

How has the industry workflow changed? I imagine every studio is using (and some abusing) these tools, but I'm interested specifically how it affects the 3D modelling, animation, and physics workflow. How do you think about the huge surge of games that can be quickly developed with these tools? Do you prototype assets using AI, then touch them up? How about animation, physics?

I find that all of these viral game demo's, on Twitter for instance, talking about "I made this game in a few hours, look how good it looks" look reductive and are not as complex as they seem. They are almost always browser based, no physics, no underlying engine like Unreal, Godot, Unity etc. My own experience making games in unreal has suggested that the LLM's still struggle with physical reasoning (ie placing objects in logical places), animation, asset generation, physical interactions etc in the absence of very specific guidance. 

Anyone here actually do game dev for a living, specifically in animation, physics, or art? How has your work changed? To what degree are these tools being used for the tasks I described?

TIA

comments.author: ananbd
comments.body:
They're not.

I work at what we believe is one of the few serious, commercial studios leaning into AI for AAA development.  We do NOT use it for creative work, full stop.  

Idealistically, I'd like to say that line is drawn on ethical grounds, but it's much simpler than that.  **AI is not creative**.  Fun games need a soul, or they fail in the market.  It's a rough landscape, and we take players' needs seriously.

But for anything "mechanical?"  It's great.  Speeds up our workflow considerably.  We apply more rigor than other areas of software development probably do, but that's inherent to games (counterintuitively, it's one of most difficult types of software development).

We use it for code generation, automation.  Anything a robot can do.

Much of this is enabled by our in-house MCP layers which interface with common game dev infrastructure.  So, that's a project in and of itself.

comments.author: delusion54
comments.body:
hi, I am a casual gamer who recently have been researching and working 12+ hours daily for 2 game projects in godot. I really think I should have subscribed earlier to tripo or meshy. Gpt astra with higgsfield blender mcp used before, was pretty tough to achieve proper results, especially hands, joints and faces of imaginary creatures. Also very computationally heavy(thus expensive). I am using tripo but rigging is probably better on meshy.

I believe the best you can do beyond that, is focus on creating high quality custom SKILLS. Define specific processes and ensure NON-CONFLICTING trigger of this skills and define expected outcomes. Auto invocation on. No more agents, just proper skills, structuring of game files and ask for md files handovers in order to maintain context per chat/thread.

comments.author: Kindly_Life_947
comments.body:
They are better. They can now even do ik animation even though it takes time and is expensive.  
Things are changing. Now its automating modeling workflows to get around issues. Creating pipelines. Human still needed to make decisions what looks good and has soul etc.
